FTSB.title: ZATCA Tax Bulletin: Tax treatment of technical or consulting services under the Income Tax Law and Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements, Version 1 (Arabic)
FTSB.note: On 23 November 2026 this ZATCA link redirected to 'page not found', so the bulletin may have been moved or withdrawn. The points below follow published summaries (KPMG GCC Tax News, 28 December 2025; Alvarez & Marsal, February 2026) and should be checked against the current ZATCA version.

OECDP.title: OECD Model Tax Convention 2025 (Full Version), Non-OECD economies' positions, Introduction, paragraph 4

PEER.title: OECD: Prevention of tax treaty abuse, Sixth peer review report on treaty shopping (Saudi Arabia)

general.t: Saudi Arabia has recorded no positions on the OECD Model or its Commentary. It is not among the 32 non-OECD economies whose positions appear in the 2025 edition, so there is no formal 'KSA commentary' on any Article. The Saudi views below come from ZATCA's own publications and Saudi Arabia's MLI choices.
ZATCA's view: treaties take precedence over domestic law, and taxpayers may claim treaty relief from domestic withholding tax, but eligibility is assessed case by case.

Relief is claimed through ZATCA's portal, either at source (reduced rate applied when paying) or by refund after withholding at the domestic rate. Both routes need a tax residency certificate in the foreign authority's own format, the request on ZATCA's form, and embassy attestation or an apostille. At source also needs an undertaking on Form Q/7C; a refund needs the payer's authorisation, the return and payment receipt, and a Chamber-attested letter. The time limit to apply or be audited is five years (Bylaws Article 66).

5.t: Most Saudi treaties include the UN-style services PE (Article 5(3)(b)): ZATCA counts 54 of the 57 treaties it had signed. The Treaty facts below show whether ZATCA lists this treaty.

ZATCA's three tests for a services PE: (1) the enterprise furnishes services through its employees or other personnel; (2) they are physically present in Saudi Arabia ('within' the State); (3) presence exceeds the treaty threshold, which varies between more than 182 days, 183 days or 6 months in any 12-month period.

Examples: a Dutch consultant's employee on site in Saudi Arabia for more than 200 days, and a UK trainer present about 204 days in the year, both create a PE. A Vietnamese company serving a Saudi client entirely online, and an Egyptian consultancy on site for 4 months under a 6-month threshold, do not.
Where a PE exists, only profits attributable to it are taxed (unless the treaty has a force-of-attraction rule), on a net basis under the Income Tax Law.
Example: online consultancy by a treaty resident with no PE in Saudi Arabia is taxable only in the residence State under the business profits Article.

Through the MLI, Saudi Arabia adopted Article 12 (agents and commissionaire arrangements), Article 13 Option A with the anti-fragmentation rule (preparatory or auxiliary activities), Article 14 (splitting-up of contracts) and Article 15 (closely related persons). These apply only where the treaty partner made matching choices.
Saudi Arabia notified the existing agency and specific-activity paragraphs in its covered treaties, for example Article 5(5) and 5(4), as the provisions the MLI rules would replace.

7.t: ZATCA treats Article 7 as the rule that decides whether a service fee or other payment is taxable in Saudi Arabia: the residence State taxes unless the non-resident has a PE in Saudi Arabia, and then only the attributable profits.

Where no PE exists, the non-resident's income from services for Saudi customers is outside Saudi income tax. Withholding tax may still apply in particular cases, for example where a treaty treats technical services as royalties.

ZATCA's 2021 circular confirms the domestic force-of-attraction rule. It says 14 treaties contain a similar rule: Azerbaijan, Bangladesh, Ethiopia, Georgia, Jordan, Kazakhstan, Mexico, North Macedonia, Tunisia, Ukraine, the UAE, Uzbekistan, Venezuela and Vietnam. Under the other treaties then in force, only profits directly attributable to the PE are taxable.

10.t: ZATCA's reading: Saudi Arabia keeps the right to tax dividends at source, and the treaty rate is granted only to the beneficial owner. A conduit company that just passes dividends on is not the beneficial owner, so the domestic rate applies, for example where a company in State X passes dividends on to an owner in State Y, which has no treaty with Saudi Arabia.

Beneficial owner, though undefined in the treaties, generally means the person who can use and enjoy the dividend without a contractual or legal obligation to pass it on. This matches the OECD Commentary test.
Saudi Arabia reserved against MLI Article 8 (dividend transfer transactions), so the MLI's 365-day holding rule for reduced dividend rates does not apply to its treaties.

11.t: First decide whether the payment is interest (Article 11) or business profits (Article 7). Under ZATCA's reading, interest requires remuneration from money lent and covers income from debt-claims of every kind, including government securities, bonds and debentures, with their premiums and prizes.
Penalty charges for late payment are not interest under the Article.

Where a treaty gives the residence State the exclusive right to tax interest, no Saudi withholding applies to a beneficial owner without a Saudi PE. If the debt-claim is effectively connected with a Saudi PE, Saudi Arabia may tax.

12.t: First decide whether a payment is a royalty (Article 12) or business profits (Article 7). Most Saudi treaties define royalties, often including payments for the use of, or right to use, industrial, commercial or scientific equipment.

ZATCA notes that the royalty scope may extend to software use, equipment leasing, container rentals and live sports broadcasts, depending on the treaty. Payments not made 'for the use of, or the right to use' a right are business profits. Payments for the use of rights, including transfers of know-how, are generally royalties.
Domestically, the sale of full ownership of industrial or intellectual property is excluded from the royalty category, which is consistent with the OECD distinction between alienation and use.

A few treaties treat technical services as royalties under Article 12: Egypt, Ethiopia, Gabon, Georgia, Malaysia, Morocco and Vietnam. Withholding then applies to the gross payment, usually at a reduced treaty rate.

ZATCA's December 2025 bulletin, as summarised: technical and consulting services usually fall under Article 7, so they are taxable in Saudi Arabia only if attributable to a PE. Some treaties include them in royalties or have a separate fees-for-technical-services article, in which case withholding tax may apply at the treaty rate. The bulletin also distinguishes technical or consulting services from transfers of know-how, which matters for whether Article 12 applies.

12A.t: Some treaties have a separate fees-for-technical-services article (generally Article 12A, following the UN Model). Such fees may then be taxed in Saudi Arabia as the source State, capped at the treaty rate for a beneficial owner resident in the other State. Otherwise technical services normally fall under Article 7.
The December 2025 bulletin (as summarised) points to dedicated technical-services articles as one of the cases where withholding tax applies to technical or consulting services under a treaty.

21.t: We found no ZATCA guidance specific to the Other income Article in the circulars listed here. Check the treaty wording: many Saudi treaties add a UN-style paragraph letting the source State tax other income.

25.t: Most Saudi treaties require a MAP request within three years of the first notification of the action. The Syria treaty allows two years and is not modified by the MLI. The treaties with France, Italy, Russia and the UK also had two years but are modified by the MLI. ZATCA cannot accept late requests and has no power to extend the deadline.

The risk of taxation contrary to the treaty must be probable, not merely possible. A case can arise from an assessment, an audit position or a withholding certificate, and self-initiated adjustments made in good faith also qualify.

The request must be dated, signed and documented: identities, treaty articles relied on, facts, amounts, analysis, and copies of assessments and objections. Requests for more information must be answered within 30 days, or the case may be delayed or closed.

MAP can run alongside domestic remedies, but the domestic case must be frozen or suspended (at the Settlement Committee or the tax committees). ZATCA follows final judicial decisions and tells the other competent authority.

ZATCA aims to resolve cases within two years. Almost all Saudi treaties implement agreements notwithstanding domestic time limits. Those with Mexico, Switzerland and the UK have specific time limits, but the UK and Mexico limits are removed by the MLI.
For Saudi Arabia, taxes covered may include income tax and zakat. Penalties and interest are excluded.

Through the MLI, Saudi Arabia adopted Article 16 (MAP minimum standard, including presenting a case to either State) and Article 17 (corresponding adjustments). It did not opt for mandatory arbitration (MLI Part VI).

29.t: Saudi Arabia adopted MLI Article 6 (the new preamble on not creating opportunities for non-taxation or treaty shopping, including optional paragraph 3) and Article 7(1), the principal purposes test, without a limitation-on-benefits rule.
OECD peer reviews record that Saudi Arabia implements the treaty-abuse minimum standard through the preamble and the PPT.

Saudi Arabia notified 18 covered treaties as already containing an anti-abuse provision of the kind the PPT replaces or supplements, for example the UK (Article 28), India (Article 26(2)), Italy (Article 29) and Japan (Article 24). The Treaty facts below show whether this treaty is one of them.
ZATCA's beneficial-ownership approach to conduit companies works alongside the PPT. A treaty resident that merely passes income on to a non-treaty owner does not get the treaty rate.
